name: Primary Hyperoxaluria Type II

criteria.description: Identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in the GRHPR gene
Elevated urinary oxalate excretion above age-adjusted reference range
Reduced or absent glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase enzyme activity in liver biopsy or fibroblasts
Recurrent nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis starting in childhood or early adulthood

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of biallelic pathogenic GRHPR variants plus elevated urinary oxalate excretion and clinical features consistent with nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Enzyme assay may support diagnosis but is not mandatory if genetic testing is conclusive.

occasional.symptomName: Fatigue related to chronic kidney disease
Bone pain due to secondary hyperparathyroidism

rare.symptomName: Peripheral neuropathy secondary to oxalate deposition

laboratory: Normal or mildly elevated plasma oxalate levels
Reduced glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase enzyme activity
imaging: Renal ultrasound showing nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones
CT scan confirming calcium oxalate calculi
Occasional evidence of systemic oxalate deposition in advanced disease
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in the GRHPR gene
other: Histopathology of kidney stones confirming calcium oxalate composition

distinguishingFeatures: Mutation in AGXT gene instead of GRHPR
Earlier onset and more severe systemic oxalosis
History of enteric disease or dietary oxalate excess
Oxalate elevation secondary to gastrointestinal malabsorption

redFlags: Early onset recurrent kidney stones in childhood
Rapid progression to end-stage renal disease
Evidence of systemic oxalate deposition (e.g., cardiac or retinal involvement)
references: Hoppe B, et al. Primary hyperoxaluria. N Engl J Med. 2009;360(6):545-553.
Williams EL, et al. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2: clinical features and genotype-phenotype correlations. Kidney Int. 2009;75(12):1314-1320.
